title: Don't Build Slop (4 Levels of AI Agent Maturity) - Ara Khan, Cline

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 78%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core subject is how to architect agents as state machines with five rules for building custom agent harnesses across four maturity levels. Cline is a coding assistant and the talk extensively references coding agent tools (Codex, Cursor, Claude Code) and developer platform concerns. The four-level maturity model progresses from framework prototyping through custom agent development to cloud deployment. Prerequisites include state machine knowledge, agent framework familiarity, CLI/CI-CD experience, and frontier model API usage, targeting intermediate practitioners. A structured conference presentation at the AI Engineer channel with timestamped sections and audience Q&A. All evidence anchors are graded said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the transcript.

summary: Ara Khan diagnoses a 'mass psychosis' in AI agent-building where developers feel paralyzed between deploying agent swarms and manually reviewing code. He proposes four levels of agent maturity. Level 1 uses existing frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph) for rapid prototyping and PMF validation but lacks customizability for production. Level 2 involves building custom agents following five rules: (1) treat every agent as a state machine—a recursive while loop with conditions and end states; (2) keep system prompts minimal because every addition risks making the agent worse—the GPT-5.3 prompt is one-third the size of GPT-5's due to sensory overload from long prompts, and Cline was rewritten from scratch about seven times to prune bloat; (3) integrate with a CLI for a pseudo-RL pipeline so other coding agents can build, test, and modify your agent; (4) don't build slop—spend time on architecture and state machine design before letting models generate code; (5) master frontier model APIs, including reasoning traces that must be sent in exact expected formats—failing to do so silently degrades performance with no way of knowing, and API asymmetries make tools like Open Router insufficient. Level 3 adopts Kanban boards as the optimal UX form factor. Because agents are inference-bound (running 8-10 minutes), users naturally run multiple in parallel. Kanban makes users engineering managers overseeing agent ICs, with a headline view and the ability to define flows. Khan made this prediction on March 26; Claude Code shipped the same feature ten hours before the talk. Level 4 ships agents to the cloud, enabling complete parallelization with separate machines per agent, no local dependencies, and long-running tasks (15-60 minutes) including autonomous UI testing. Khan's final vision: Kanban for UX, cloud for compute. In Q&A, he demonstrates that Kanban tasks show full traces and transition states (in progress → review) when agents need human input.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Every agent is a state machine: a recursive while loop with conditions and end states—visualizing this mental model makes building and debugging easier.
Every addition to an agent risks making it worse; frontier models perform better with minimal system prompts—GPT-5.3's prompt is one-third the size of GPT-5's due to sensory overload.
Failing to use frontier model APIs in the exact precise way (including reasoning trace formats) silently degrades performance with no way of knowing; API asymmetries make Open Router insufficient.
Agents are inference-bound (8-10 minutes), so users naturally run multiple in parallel; Kanban boards are the optimal UX form factor, making users engineering managers overseeing agent ICs.
Khan predicted Kanban UX on March 26; Claude Code shipped the same feature ten hours before his talk.
Cloud agents enable complete parallelization with separate machines, no local dependencies, and long-running autonomous tasks including UI/QA testing (15-60 minutes).
Architecture and state machine design must be done thoughtfully by humans; don't let models blindly generate agent code without design oversight.
The four maturity levels serve as rough heuristics—start with the bare minimum and slide up or down based on effort investment.
Kanban task interfaces show full execution traces and transition states (in progress → review) when agents need human input, enabling effective planning and back-and-forth requirements gathering.
Cline has been rewritten from scratch approximately seven times to remove accumulated bloat.

sections.title: Introduction: Mass Psychosis in Agent-Building
sections.summary: Khan addresses the overwhelming confusion developers feel about agents—whether to deploy many agents or manually review code. He shows three indistinguishable UIs from Factory, Codex, and Cursor to illustrate that everything looks the same, motivating the need to build your own well-architected agents.

sections.title: Four Levels of Agent Maturity Overview
sections.summary: Outlines the four levels: using frameworks for prototyping, building custom agents as state machines, adopting Kanban UX workflows, and shipping to the cloud.

sections.title: Level 1: Using Existing Agent Frameworks
sections.summary: Frameworks like LangChain and LangGraph are great for finding PMF and getting something working in 30 minutes, but they lack the customizability and modularity needed for serious production work.

sections.title: Level 2: Building Your Own Agents (Rules 1-5)
sections.summary: Introduces five rules for writing custom agent code, beginning with Rule 1: treat every agent as a state machine—a while loop with conditions and end states—so you always have a mental model of agent state.

sections.title: Rule 2: Keep It Simple—Every Addition Risks Making It Worse
sections.summary: Frontier models perform better with fewer instructions. The GPT-5.3 prompt is one-third the size of GPT-5's. Long system prompts cause sensory overload. Cline was rewritten from scratch about seven times to prune bloat.

sections.title: Rule 3: Integrate with CLI for a Pseudo-RL Pipeline
sections.summary: Agents should have a CLI so other coding agents can build, test, and modify them autonomously. This enables long-running parallel agents to make and validate changes, creating a pseudo-RL feedback loop.

sections.title: Rule 4: Don't Build Slop
sections.summary: Spend time thinking through architecture and design before letting models generate code. The architecture and state machine design must be done thoughtfully by humans, even when using agents to assist.

sections.title: Rule 5: Master Frontier Model APIs (Reasoning Traces)
sections.summary: Frontier Labs' APIs create lock-in by making interchangeability harder. Newer models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-5.3) use reasoning traces that must be sent in exact expected formats. Failing to do so silently degrades performance with no way of knowing. API asymmetries mean tools like Open Router are insufficient; developers must carefully test each frontier lab's API individually.

sections.title: Level 3: The UX Form Factor—Kanban Boards
sections.summary: Khan argues Kanban boards are the optimal UX form factor for agents. Because agents are inference-bound (8-10 minutes), users naturally run multiple in parallel, potentially mutating the same source. Kanban provides isolation of state, a headline-level view, and flow control—making users engineering managers with agents as ICs. Khan made this prediction on March 26; Claude Code shipped the same feature ten hours before the talk.

sections.title: Level 4: Shipping to the Cloud for Scalability
sections.summary: Cloud agents enable complete parallelization with separate machines per agent and no local dependencies. They can run very long tasks (15-60 minutes) including autonomous UI/QA testing—clicking through interfaces, changing settings, testing in terminals, and iterating on failures. This enables scalable distribution across large organizations and easy task dispatch from phones or laptops with PRs ready when returning to a workstation.

sections.title: Final Synthesis and Closing
sections.summary: Khan's final vision: Kanban for UX, cloud for compute. The four levels serve as rough heuristics—start with the bare minimum easy thing and slide up or down based on desired effort investment. He invites questions and engagement.

sections.title: Q&A: Planning and State Transitions in Kanban
sections.summary: Audience question about planning and requirements gathering in Kanban. Khan demonstrates that each Kanban task shows the full execution trace. Users can have a conversation with the agent, then pull out when it can work independently. Tasks transition from 'in progress' to 'review' state when the agent needs human input, enabling effective back-and-forth planning.
